newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airlines body to fight British noise limits.
newsitem.headline: Airlines body to fight British noise limits.

text.p: The global airlines body IATA said on Monday it would launch a quick judicial challenge against a new British rule reducing noise limits for departing aircraft to go into effect at London's airports on January 1.

Pierre Jeanniot, Director-General of the International Air Transport Association, told a news conference the initial aim of the action would be to "get a judge to put a stay on the rule", decreed by Britain's Department of Transport.

"These very stringent restrictions would affect nearly every airline operating into and out of London," said Jeanniot. "Even the most modern aircraft would not be able to conform if they take off with a full load.
"We cannot understand how the British government can have taken such a decision without any consultation with the industry."
The decision to take legal action to try to halt implementation of the new rule, announced at the end of the summer, was taken by the IATA board at a meeting on Sunday.
The board, which includes executives from major world airlines including British Airways PLC, said in a statement the decision was "of very serious concern."
There was no immediate comment from BA itself, whose IATA board member is Chief Executive Robert Ayling.

It could have "far reaching consequences for civil aviation operations in other parts of the world," declared the statement -- presented on Monday to the annual general meeting of the Geneva- and Montreal-based IATA.

Fears that the British action -- applying to Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted airports -- might have a snowball effect elsewhere were also voiced at the news conference by Juergen Weber, chairman of Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
"We felt that this move could set a very bad example, and bring new limitations on our business at the airport level elsewhere in the world," he said.

Under the rule, noise limits for aircraft departing from the three London airports are to be reduced by three decibels to 94 decibels between 7.a.m. and 11 p.m. and by two decibels for night operations from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.
The British Transport Ministry has also proposed a new high-priority study into the feasibility of also setting new noise limits for landing aircraft.

Weber said the British authorities appeared to be taking little account of the efforts airlines were taking to cut noise levels. "We feel the quietness of our aircraft is not being recognised," the Lufthansa executive said.

Jeanniot told the news conference the new levels were set so low that airlines would have little choice but to violate them on almost every take-off, and so incur the heavy fines provided for under the new rules.
"Additional costs of this type would be an extra burden at a time when we are facing rapidly rising fuel costs," said one IATA official.
He said the new costs would make it more difficult for the airlines to invest in the latest aircraft, whose noise levels are generally lower than those of most planes currently in service.
